strengths: Well-motivated problem: Addresses genuine limitation in generative models' inability to render physically-plausible refractions where refracted pixels constrain observed surfaces through optical principles.

Principled technical approach: Sound integration of Snell's Law (Eq. 7-8), ray tracing, and Fresnel equations (Eq. 12-13) into diffusion generation pipeline with proper total internal reflection handling.

Comprehensive system design: Clever cross-view synchronization strategy using panoramic generation to handle occluded/out-of-view surfaces, with thoughtful integration of Laplacian pyramid warping and time travel.

Strong qualitative results: Clear visual improvements over Flux baselines with physically-plausible left-right/up-down flips and radial distortion matching Blender references across diverse object geometries.

Thorough experimental validation: Quantitative improvements (PSNR 17.10 vs 11.24, LPIPS 0.28 vs 0.51), ablation study demonstrating each component's necessity, sensitivity analysis across refractive indices, and extended results on diverse shapes.
Good reproducibility: Detailed implementation specifications, full text prompts in supplementary, clear algorithmic descriptions, and well-documented hyperparameters.
weaknesses: Severely restrictive scope: Handles only single uniform-refractive-index transparent objects with heuristic placement; cannot model multiple objects, inhomogeneous materials, scattering, absorption, or user-controlled positioning.

Evaluation methodology concerns: Pseudo-ground truth Blender images are not harmonized for lighting and miss refracted surfaces, undermining PSNR/LPIPS metrics. Only 6 scenes with primarily glass spheres. No human perceptual studies validating physical plausibility claims.

Cascading external dependencies: Requires 3D model generation (TRELLIS), LLM-based refractive index queries (unreliable for unfamiliar materials), depth estimation (MoGe-2), and post-processing relighting model—each a potential failure point without robustness analysis.

Unvalidated panorama consistency: Panoramic image independently generated and hallucinated to fill unseen surfaces; synchronization doesn't guarantee geometric consistency with perspective view. Limited systematic analysis of when/why panorama quality degrades.

Limited technical novelty: Synchronization framework heavily adapted from prior work (SyncTweedies, LookingGlass, Visual Anagrams); Laplacian pyramid warping and time travel directly from LookingGlass. Contribution is primarily application rather than methodological innovation.
Computational cost not addressed: 126 seconds per image-pair on A100 GPU with no speedup analysis, scalability discussion, or practical feasibility assessment compared to standard generation.

Incomplete technical justification: Blending strategy (Eq. 10) lacks theoretical foundation; no convergence guarantees for synchronizing two independent diffusion processes; no sensitivity analysis for design choices (λ=0.5, pyramid levels=5).

Missing failure analysis and edge cases: No documentation of failure modes, sensitivity to depth estimation errors, or handling of complex caustics, glancing angles, highly reflective surfaces, or partially-transparent objects.

Limited evaluation scope: All test scenes are close-up indoor views; no outdoor scenes, distant backgrounds, or complex geometry. No comparison with other physics-aware synthesis methods or geometry-constrained generation approaches.
Insufficient user control: No mechanism for interactive object placement, refractive index control, or material property specification; text-only control is coarse and indirect.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: Addresses a genuine limitation in current generative models' handling of transparent objects, clearly demonstrated through visual comparisons
Sound technical foundation: Correct application of Snell's Law, ray tracing, and Fresnel equations for optical modeling
Comprehensive technical integration: Thoughtfully combines multiple techniques (Laplacian pyramid warping, time travel, panoramic synchronization) with principled justification
Clear qualitative improvements: Figure 3 convincingly demonstrates characteristic refraction effects (directional flips, radial distortion) that baselines fail to capture
Thorough ablation studies: Both qualitative and quantitative ablations demonstrate meaningful contributions from each component
Extended object diversity: Supplement includes diverse geometries (dog, fox, pyramid) beyond illustrative sphere case
weaknesses: Critically limited evaluation scope: Only 6 text prompts total, all similar indoor scenes with identical setup. Insufficient for statistical significance and cannot support broad claims about generalizability

Invalid ground truth: Blender reference explicitly has incorrect lighting and missing geometry. Metrics (masked PSNR with histogram matching, LPIPS) measure image reconstruction, not optical accuracy. Table 2 shows Flux standard outperforms method on ImageReward (0.60 vs 0.59)

Restrictive assumptions inadequately disclosed: Single object only, homogeneous materials, no scattering, ad-hoc placement heuristic. No upfront summary or robustness analysis for assumption violations
Cascading errors unanalyzed: Method depends on TRELLIS (3D generation), MoGe-2 (depth), LLM (material properties), Flux Kontext (relighting). No robustness testing for failures in any component

Incremental technical novelty: Ray tracing with Snell's Law is standard graphics; core contribution is applying SyncTweedies/LookingGlass synchronization to refractive warping. Blending uses existing techniques. Limited fundamental algorithmic advance

Incomplete experimental validation: No user studies to validate perceived plausibility. Only Flux baselines compared; no comparison to physics-based methods or specialized reflection/refraction approaches. No failure case analysis
Mixed quantitative results undermine claims: ImageReward favors Flux standard; CLIP improvements marginal. Without user studies, claims of 'physically plausible' refractions lack support
Computational cost and scalability not addressed: ~126 seconds per image pair (2× baseline). No analysis of computational trade-offs or scaling behavior

Overstated claims: Described as 'optically-accurate' but handles only primary refraction/reflection; no caustics, absorption, subsurface scattering, or complex light transport. Claims should be more precisely qualified
Reproducibility concerns: Depends on multiple models (TRELLIS, MoGe-2, Flux Kontext) with unclear availability/versioning. Code availability not mentioned. Relighting model details sparse
Fragile object placement: Heuristic selection of 'nearest horizontal surface' cannot handle objects held by people, suspended in air, or non-standard layouts. No failure analysis
Questionable design choices lack justification: λ=0.5 blending weight, 5 Laplacian levels, panoramic view selection—all appear arbitrary without sensitivity analysis

strengths: Novel application of physics-based constraints (Snell's Law) to enforcing optical consistency in diffusion-based image generation, addressing a concrete and visually important failure mode of current models
Clever two-view synchronization approach using panoramic views to handle refracted rays reaching occluded or out-of-frame surfaces—an elegant solution to a genuine technical challenge
Training-free method operating on top of existing generative models (Flux) without requiring retraining, improving accessibility and practical adoption

Comprehensive experimental validation including qualitative results across diverse scenes and object geometries, quantitative metrics (PSNR, LPIPS) against rendered ground truth, informative ablation studies, and sensitivity analyses (refractive index, time travel parameters)

Clear presentation with effective visualizations (especially Figure 2); honest discussion of limitations and approximations; detailed implementation details and supplementary material supporting reproducibility

Demonstrated improvements over strong baselines (Flux inpainting and generation) with visibly better refraction accuracy showing correct left-right/up-down flips and radial distortions matching physical principles
weaknesses: Limited evaluation scope: only 6 text prompts and indoor scenes in main evaluation; single transparent object focus; primarily glass spheres; unclear generalization to outdoor, multi-object, or more diverse material scenarios

Strong practical constraints limiting applicability: requires 3D object model (via text-to-3D), material properties via LLM (fragile for complex materials), uniform refractive index assumption, no scattering, heuristic object placement without user control—collectively these significantly narrow the method's real-world applicability

Quantitative evaluation concerns: Blender ground truth has acknowledged issues (incorrect lighting, missing occluded regions); PSNR/LPIPS improvements are modest and measured against imperfect reference; no perceptual user study to validate that metric improvements translate to human preference

Incomplete technical robustness analysis: depth estimation error propagation to ray tracing not analyzed; reflection quality dependency on panorama quality not systematically studied; Fresnel blending validity under all viewing angles not justified; simplifying assumptions (single reflection, no scattering) not empirically validated

Limited baseline comparisons: only Flux variants compared; no comparison to other recent generative models or rendering-based approaches; baselines not designed for this task, making comparisons somewhat limited; computational cost (~126s per image) not compared against baselines

Moderate novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (SyncTweedies, LookingGlass, Snell's Law) in a novel application; the core innovation is the combination and application rather than introducing fundamentally new methods or insights

Hyperparameter sensitivity underdiscussed: many design choices (λ=0.5, pyramid levels, time travel counts) with limited principled guidance; Figure 12 shows settings matter but optimization rationale unclear

Failure modes and boundary conditions largely underdiscussed: no systematic analysis of when/why method fails; behavior with complex refractive paths, caustics, chromatic aberration, or challenging geometries unknown

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: generating images with physically accurate refraction and reflection of transparent objects, which existing generative models fail to handle well

Principled physics-based approach incorporating fundamental optical principles (Snell's Law, Fresnel equations) directly into generation, ensuring physical consistency rather than relying solely on learned priors
Novel cross-view synchronization framework cleverly combining physics constraints with generative models to ensure geometric consistency between perspective and panoramic views

Well-designed technical pipeline coherently integrating depth estimation, physics-based ray tracing, and cross-view warping with clear implementation details and hyperparameters provided

Insufficient baseline comparisons: compared only against text-to-image models (FLUX, Stable Diffusion, Qwen) not designed for physics-guided generation; no comparison with physics-informed generative methods; baseline configurations unclear

strengths: Addresses a genuine limitation in current generative models: realistic rendering of transparent objects with proper refraction and reflection, clearly motivated with compelling examples
Principled physics-based approach that explicitly integrates optical principles (Snell's Law, Fresnel equations) rather than relying solely on learning; ray tracing formulation is technically sound
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple metrics (CLIP, ImageReward, PSNR, LPIPS), four strong baselines, both synthetic and real-world image evaluation, and thorough ablation studies
Consistent improvements across scenes and metrics (Table 1), demonstrating reliable performance of the approach
Includes real-world validation (Figure 5) on actual camera-captured images, moving beyond purely synthetic benchmarks
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: flow matching, classifier-free guidance, Laplacian pyramid warping, and other components are borrowed from prior work. The contribution is primarily combining existing techniques for a specific application rather than fundamental algorithmic innovation

Evaluation metrics do not validate physical correctness of refractions: CLIP and ImageReward only measure perceptual plausibility, not whether rendered refractions obey actual optical laws. No verification against ground-truth physics simulations

No human perceptual evaluation despite claims about 'realism'; humans are the ultimate judges of plausibility and physical correctness, and automated metrics cannot distinguish physically correct from plausible-looking-but-wrong refractions

Technical clarity gaps: view synchronization mechanism inadequately explained; occlusion handling for refracted surfaces not rigorously specified; heavy dependence on depth/mask estimation quality (MoGe-2, SAM) without robustness analysis

Reproducibility concerns: no mention of code or model release; relies on multiple external components with varying availability (FLUX-dev, MoGe-2, TRELLIS, Blender, SAM); prompt engineering specificity unclear for generalization

Unfair baseline comparison: comparing against general-purpose models not designed for transparent object rendering; no comparison with other physics-aware or refraction-specific methods; unclear how much improvement derives from the specialized approach versus baseline inadequacy
